source.title: Electronic reminders and hand-hygiene compliance among nurses in three Danish hospitals: a stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial
source.abstract: Hand-hygiene compliance among hospital staff remains below recommended levels despite decades of campaigns. We conducted a stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial in three Danish hospitals between January 2025 and March 2026. Twenty-four general medical and surgical wards took part; intensive care units, operating theatres and paediatric wards were excluded because their hand-hygiene protocols differ. A total of 1,204 nurses were observed. Each ward received an electronic dispenser that emitted a two-second light signal when a staff member passed a patient bed without using it. Compliance was measured by trained observers blinded to the allocation sequence, using the World Health Organization five-moments protocol. Compliance rose from 43% at baseline to 61% after twelve weeks of the intervention (adjusted odds ratio 2.04, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.43). The effect declined to 54% by week 26, suggesting habituation to the signal. Hospital-acquired infection rates were recorded but the trial was not powered to detect a change in them.
source.tldr: Light-based electronic reminders raised nurses' hand-hygiene compliance from 43% to 61%, with the effect fading after six months.
